ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: Transistor geometries in a CMOS inverter have been adjusted to meet the requirement for worst-case charge and discharge times for driving a load capacitor \( C \). This design is to be converted to that of a NOR circuit in the same technology, so that its worst-case charge and discharge times while driving the same capacitor are similar. The channel lengths of all transistors are to be kept unchanged. Which one of the following statements is correct?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: Widths of PMOS transistors should be doubled, while widths of NMOS transistors should not be changed.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a CMOS inverter driving a load capacitor C being converted into a 2-input NOR gate driving the same capacitor. In the NOR gate, the PMOS pull-up network has two PMOS transistors in series from VDD to the output, while the NMOS pull-down network is in parallel. Reasoning: For charging the output capacitor, the inverter uses a single PMOS path with width Wp and resistance Rp. In the 2-input NOR gate, the worst-case charging path occurs when both inputs are low, so current must pass through two series PMOS transistors. Delay is approximately proportional to Req C, and C is unchanged, so the NOR pull-up equivalent resistance should match the inverter pull-up resistance. Since PMOS on-resistance scales approximately inversely with width, doubling each PMOS width makes each PMOS resistance Rp/2. Two such PMOS resistances in series give Rp/2 + Rp/2 = Rp, matching the inverter charging resistance.

method.method_draft: Identify the worst-case charging path. In the inverter, the capacitor charges through a single PMOS of width Wp. In the 2-input NOR, the output charges only when both inputs are low, so current passes through two series PMOS transistors. Since delay is approximately 0.69 R_eq C and C is unchanged, set the NOR series pull-up resistance equal to the inverter pull-up resistance. Because each PMOS resistance scales inversely with width, doubling each PMOS width halves each device resistance; two such half-resistances in series equal the original one-resistor path. Therefore each PMOS width should be doubled.

method.method_draft: Treat the conversion as a standard-cell sizing problem. The inverter is already sized to meet the load timing. In a 2-input NOR, the critical rising transition is through a two-transistor PMOS series stack. Standard equal-drive sizing says that every device in a series stack should be multiplied by the number of stacked devices to compensate for the reduced pull-up strength. Since the PMOS stack has two devices, choose each PMOS width to be twice the inverter PMOS width.

Image description: The figure shows a CMOS inverter driving a load capacitor C being converted into a 2-input NOR gate. In the NOR gate, the pull-up network consists of two PMOS transistors in series from VDD to the output, while the pull-down network consists of NMOS transistors in parallel.

Reasoning: The original inverter was sized so its single PMOS provides the required worst-case charging time for capacitor C. In a 2-input NOR, the worst-case rising transition charges C through two series PMOS devices. If their widths stayed the same, the effective pull-up resistance would roughly double, slowing the charge time. Since MOS on-resistance is approximately inversely proportional to channel width, making each PMOS twice as wide halves each device resistance. Two half-resistances in series then give approximately the same resistance as the original inverter PMOS. Therefore, each PMOS in the NOR should be doubled in width relative to the inverter PMOS.
